title: R&B/Hip-Hop Power Players: Billboard’s 2026 List Revealed
summary: Nominated by their companies and chosen by Billboard editors, these are the executives within both genres leading the field this year.
contentText:
Above Ground Entertainment CEO David Ali leads Billboard ’s list of executives across multiple industry sectors pushing the genres forward.

Bass is concerned about “the lack of creative growth” she’s seeing in R&B and hip-hop today. “We have to continue to innovate and push the culture forward.”

Bass and Bouab — co-­presidents of the Atlantic Music Group division 300 Entertainment, as well as co-presidents of hip-hop, R&B and global music at Atlantic Records — are dedicated to making good on that mission. Over the last 18 months, a parade of artists across both Atlantic’s and 300’s label rosters has notched multiple career milestones.

Before launching her anticipated Little Miss Drama Tour earlier this year, Cardi B watched her long-awaited sophomore album, Am I the Drama? (which has now surpassed 2.2 billion official on-demand global streams for its songs since its release, according to Luminate) debut atop the Billboard 200 last October and launch 14 songs onto the Billboard Hot 100 . Hitting the arena circuit in February, the rap superstar’s tour wrapped in April with a gross of more than $70 million and 453,000 tickets sold, according to Billboard Boxscore.

Atlantic’s Don Toliver also posted wins for the label. Toliver’s fifth studio album, Octane , became his first Billboard 200 chart-topper, and the first leg of his Octane arena world tour began in May and ended in July; the second started Aug. 4 and will wrap in London in November.

Meanwhile, the Kehlani whirlwind is in full force. “Folded,” the singer-­songwriter’s first No. 1 on Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs and first top 10 on the Hot 100, won two Grammys (best R&B song and best R&B solo performance). The track helped propel Kehlani’s 2026 self-titled album to a No. 4 debut on the Billboard 200 in May.

At 300 Entertainment, Gunna’s latest project, The Last Wun , landed at No. 1 on Top Rap Albums and Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums — his sixth time to reign on both. The album, which includes the Burna Boy-featuring “WGFT,” also reached No. 3 on the Billboard 200. Meanwhile, fellow 300 Entertainment artist Fetty Wap orchestrated a comeback this year following his early release from prison, dropping his fourth album, Zavier , in March.

“Fetty Wap coming home, releasing new music and being shown the love and recognition he deserves was one of my favorite musical moments,” Bass says. “He’s legendary, and his music will resonate for generations.”

Looking ahead to the rest of the year and 2027, Bass adds, “There’s some incredible music being created across the roster and new partnerships to be announced that will continue to drive our success.” —Gail Mitchell

T.I.

Before this year, many people thought the best days of T.I.’s career were behind him: The owner of four Hot 100 No. 1 singles and three Billboard 200 No. 1 albums hadn’t released a project in six years and hadn’t reached the top half of the Hot 100 in over a decade. But his breezy, braggadocious 2026 single, “Let ’Em Know,” turned back the clock for Tip and reminded hip-hop fans that the man who once called himself “King” wasn’t dead yet.

Released in January, “Let ‘Em Know” enjoyed a gradual run up the charts driven by word-of-mouth and organic marketing, ultimately reaching No. 8 on Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs, No. 1 on Mainstream R&B/Hip-Hop Airplay and a No. 33 peak on the Hot 100 in April — the first time T.I. reached the top 40 since 2014.

It was a welcome return for one of Atlanta’s elder statesmen and ­heralded the comeback of his own Grand Hustle imprint, which he’s cultivated for years. “Grand Hustle’s complete transition into true independence and the commercial success we’ve achieved on our own terms” is how Tip characterized the achievement, which he calls his proudest moment of the year. ­Another highlight: “Being able to open up the BET Awards with ‘Let ’Em Know’ with my son King and my patna Young Dro in front of an audience of my peers was amazing.”

For now, Tip says that the album Kill the King , released in June, will be his last — but that doesn’t mean he’ll stop having fun and playing music. He’s spent the summer on the road with his sons King and Domani for his King Succession Tour, while going forward he’ll be putting in work supporting his Grand Hustle artists P$C, Buddy Red, T.O Green, Joe Green and more. “Seeing them put in the work on a nightly basis has made me proud,” he says. “The future of Grand Hustle remains bright.” —Dan Rys

Erving

Courtesy of The Orchard

If the past two years have taught anything, it’s that patience and dedication to the craft can pay off — even outside the confines of the traditional industry.

That has long been where Erving, who heads the Orchard-­distributed Human Re Sources, has operated. In RAYE — an uber-talented singer-­songwriter who washed out of the major-label system and discovered peace and freedom in the indie world — he found the perfect partner.
